period_summary: Citations are heavily concentrated in the 2nd–4th centuries CE, reflecting the verse's central role in early Christological debates about Christ's divine sonship, session at God's right hand, and messianic identity. This passage is among the most frequently cited OT texts in patristic literature.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου
citations.text_form_note: Justin's citation precisely matches the LXX Greek text with κύριος for both YHWH and אדני, κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν, and ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν. No evidence of influence from Hebrew or alternative Greek versions.
citations.theological_use: Justin employs this verse extensively to prove Christ's pre-existence and divine lordship against Trypho's Jewish objections, arguing that the doubled 'Lord' demonstrates two divine persons and that the session at God's right hand occurred after the ascension.
citations.transmission_implication: Attests the stability of the LXX text form in Rome by the mid-2nd century, already functioning as authoritative Christian scripture.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus cites through the Vetus Latina (Old Latin), which is a direct translation of the LXX. The Latin 'Dominus Domino meo' and 'sede a dextris' reflect Greek κύριος/κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν, not the Hebrew.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus uses the verse to establish the dual nature of Christ—the one seated is fully human (Son of David), the one commanding is God the Father, demonstrating Christ's exaltation after incarnation and passion.
citations.transmission_implication: Confirms LXX-based tradition was transmitted to Gaul via Latin translation by late 2nd century, showing geographical spread of the Septuagintal text form.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus Domino meo, Sede ad dexteram meam, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin citation follows the LXX pattern with doubled 'Dominus' and 'sede ad dexteram' (sit at right hand). Minor variation 'ad dexteram' vs. 'a dextris' reflects Latin translation fluidity, not Hebrew influence.
citations.theological_use: Tertullian deploys the verse polemically against Marcion to prove continuity between Creator God of OT and Father of Jesus, showing that the God who exalts Christ is the same God of the Psalms.
citations.transmission_implication: North African Latin tradition by early 3rd century consistently reflects LXX Vorlage, suggesting standardized transmission through Greek intermediary.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου
citations.text_form_note: Origen cites the standard LXX text but was aware of Hebrew and other Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) through his Hexapla. His commentary notes that all Greek versions agree on this rendering, distinguishing it from Hebrew ambiguity.
citations.theological_use: Origen interprets allegorically and literally: Christ sits at right hand signifying honor and power, while enemies as footstool represents complete subjugation of hostile powers, ultimately pointing to eschatological victory.
citations.transmission_implication: Despite Hexaplaric knowledge of multiple text forms, Origen confirms LXX as the ecclesiastically received text, showing its dominance even where alternatives were known.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου, ἕως ἂν θῶ τοὺς ἐχθρούς σου ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν σου
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius reproduces the standard LXX verbatim across multiple works. His access to Origen's Hexapla library confirms this was the deliberate choice of the ecclesiastical text, not ignorance of alternatives.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius uses the verse extensively in anti-Arian polemic to prove Christ's distinct hypostasis and divine dignity, arguing that the Father's command to 'sit' demonstrates relational distinction within the Godhead while affirming Christ's equality through shared throne.
citations.transmission_implication: Early 4th-century Caesarea maintained strict adherence to LXX despite hexaplaric manuscript availability, indicating ecclesial preference stabilized transmission.

citations.cited_text: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου· κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου
citations.text_form_note: Athanasius consistently cites the LXX form with both κύριος terms and discusses the theological implications of each. He shows no awareness of or interest in Hebrew text differences, treating LXX as inspired scripture.
citations.theological_use: Central to Athanasian Christology: the verse proves Christ's eternal Sonship (not adopted), his consubstantiality with Father (seated at right hand = equal honor), and his distinct personhood (Father addresses Son), directly refuting Arian subordinationism.
citations.transmission_implication: Mid-4th century Alexandria treated LXX Psalm text as theologically normative and textually stable, forming doctrinal foundation without textual variance concerns.

citations.text_form_note: Chrysostom cites standard LXX text and exegetes it phrase by phrase in the Antiochene literal-historical method. No variants noted; his homiletical exposition assumes textual fixity and congregation familiarity with this exact wording.
citations.theological_use: Chrysostom emphasizes the verse as David's prophetic testimony to Christ's divine-human nature, using 'my Lord' to show David's recognition of messianic superiority, and the session to demonstrate post-ascension glory without denying Christ's ongoing divine nature.
citations.transmission_implication: Late 4th-century Antioch/Constantinople liturgical and homiletical use confirms LXX text was universally known and stable in Eastern churches' public worship.

citations.cited_text: Dixit Dominus Domino meo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum
citations.text_form_note: Augustine cites through Old Latin (Vetus Latina) based on LXX, with 'Dominus Domino' reflecting Greek κύριος rendering of both Hebrew divine names. He occasionally references Jerome's Hebraicum but defaults to traditional Latin-LXX for theological exposition.
citations.theological_use: Augustine interprets the verse ecclesiologically and eschatologically: Christ's session represents his current reign through the Church, with enemies as footstool signifying gradual subjugation of evil through gospel proclamation, completed at final judgment.
citations.transmission_implication: Early 5th-century North Africa shows tension between emerging Vulgate (from Hebrew) and traditional LXX-based Old Latin, but LXX form remained dominant in liturgy and commentary.

transmission_synthesis: The patristic citation evidence for Psalm 110:1 reveals remarkable textual uniformity: all eight fathers cited (spanning Rome, Gaul, North Africa, Alexandria, Caesarea, Antioch, Constantinople) consistently use the LXX text form with no attestation of MT-based or independent readings. The LXX's distinctive double κύριος (for YHWH and Adonai), κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν (sit at right hand), and ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν (footstool of your feet) appear universally without variation across geographical and linguistic boundaries (Greek and Latin). Even text-critical scholars like Origen and Jerome-aware Augustine, who had access to Hebrew and alternative Greek versions, consistently cite and exposit the LXX form in their theological works, indicating ecclesial standardization. This uniformity strongly supports a single, stable LXX transmission stream that became fixed as authoritative Christian scripture by the mid-2nd century and remained unchanged through 5th century despite knowledge of Hebrew divergences. The theological centrality of this verse in Christological debates (anti-Jewish, anti-Arian, Chalcedonian discussions) likely contributed to conservative textual transmission, as any variation would have doctrinal implications.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Early Christian writers from across the Roman world—whether writing in Greek or Latin, in Rome, North Africa, or the Eastern Mediterranean—all cite Psalm 110:1 in exactly the same form, based on the Greek Septuagint translation. Despite some scholars knowing Hebrew and alternative translations, the Greek version became so firmly established as Christian scripture by the 100s CE that it was transmitted without change for centuries, likely because it was central to Christian beliefs about Jesus as divine and seated at God's right hand.

notable_variants.reading: κάθου ἐκ δεξιῶν μου (sit at my right hand) - LXX standard
notable_variants.significance: This LXX rendering became the universal Christian text despite Hebrew שֵׁב לִימִינִי being potentially ambiguous. The Greek formulation supported early Christological claims about Christ's exaltation and equality with God, making it theologically indispensable and thus textually conservative.

notable_variants.reading: Εἶπεν ὁ κύριος τῷ κυρίῳ μου (The Lord said to my Lord) - double κύριος
notable_variants.significance: The LXX's translation of both יהוה (YHWH) and אֲדֹנִי (Adonai) as κύριος created the 'two Lords' formulation that became exegetically crucial for patristic Christology, enabling arguments for Christ's distinct divine personhood. This theological utility ensured this exact Greek wording was preserved without deviation across all patristic citations.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Absolute LXX Uniformity Despite Hexaplaric Alternatives Available
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The most striking finding is zero textual variation among patristic citations despite demonstrated knowledge of Hebrew and alternative Greek versions (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) in centers like Caesarea and by scholars like Origen. Even Augustine, aware of Jerome's Hebrew-based Vulgate, retains the LXX-based Old Latin. This suggests the LXX text of Ps 110:1 achieved 'canonical' fixity in Christian use by mid-2nd century not through ignorance of alternatives but through deliberate theological preference. The verse's centrality to Christological arguments created conservative transmission pressure: any textual variation would destabilize doctrinal prooftexts, so the LXX form was preserved with exceptional fidelity across five centuries and vast geographical dispersion.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Church fathers kept citing Psalm 110:1 in exactly the same Greek form for over 300 years, even when they knew other versions existed, because this specific wording was essential to Christian beliefs about Jesus. The verse was too theologically important to change, so it was copied with unusual care.
